lessons.title: What stakeholders are
lessons.html:
What stakeholders are

A stakeholder is any person, group or organisation that affects the business or is affected by it. Customers are stakeholders, but there are many others. A seed company that only thinks about its customers may run into trouble with workers, regulators, growers or the community.

Internal stakeholders

Internal stakeholders are inside the business:

  • Owners and shareholders, who want profit and growth.
  • Directors and managers, who set direction and are responsible for results.
  • Employees, from breeders and lab analysts to processing workers and sales staff, who want fair pay, safe work and development.
  • Departments, such as production, processing, laboratory, sales and finance, which depend on each other.
  • Trade unions representing employees, where present.

External stakeholders

StakeholderInterest in a seed business
Customers (farmers, co-ops, dealers)Quality seed, fair prices, good service
Contract seed growersFair contracts, timely payment, technical support
SuppliersOrders and payment for packaging, chemicals, equipment
Government departments and regulatorsCompliance with seed, plant health, labour and tax laws
Industry bodies (e.g. SANSOR)Industry standards and certification
Research institutionsCooperation on cultivar testing and research
Banks and financiersLoan repayment and business stability
Local communityJobs, safe operations, no pollution
CompetitorsMarket share; also share industry issues

Stakeholders can have different and even conflicting interests. Shareholders may want lower costs, while employees want higher wages. Growers want high prices for seed crops, while the sales team wants competitive seed prices. Managing a business means balancing these interests. A business that keeps its most important stakeholders informed and treats them fairly usually finds it easier to solve problems when they come.

lessons.title: Identifying and working with stakeholders
lessons.html:
Identifying and working with stakeholders

For any project or activity, it helps to list the stakeholders and decide how to deal with each one. For example, if the company plans to build a new seed processing plant near a rural town, stakeholders include the municipality, neighbouring farmers, the local community, the environmental authorities, employees who may move, and suppliers.

Steps to identify stakeholders

  1. Describe the activity or decision clearly.
  2. Ask: who will be affected? Who can influence the outcome? Who has information we need?
  3. List internal and external stakeholders.
  4. For each, note their interest and how much influence they have.
  5. Decide how to communicate and involve them.

Influence and interest

Low interestHigh interest
High influenceKeep satisfied (e.g. bank)Manage closely (e.g. regulator, major customer)
Low influenceMonitor (e.g. general public)Keep informed (e.g. local community members)

Communication with stakeholders

  • Choose the right channel: meetings, reports, newsletters, farmer days, WhatsApp groups for growers, or official letters to regulators.
  • Use language the stakeholder understands. Technical terms suit a breeder but not a community meeting.
  • Be honest and consistent. Promises made to one stakeholder affect others.
  • Record important communications and agreements.

Your role

Even if you are not a manager, you deal with stakeholders every day: a grower on the phone, an inspector at the gate, a supplier delivering bags. Treat them professionally and pass important information to the right person in the business.

Key points

  • Stakeholders affect or are affected by the business.
  • Internal stakeholders include owners, managers, employees and departments.
  • External stakeholders include customers, growers, suppliers, regulators, banks and the community.
  • Stakeholders may have conflicting interests that must be balanced.
  • Map interest and influence to decide how to communicate.
